blocks.text: Connections drop.
A network blips, a local server crashes, a remote service restarts.
None of that has to mean the end of a session, reconnection strategies are what let a client recover and keep going instead of simply giving up.
1. Reconnecting Is Not the Same as the Original Connect

blocks.alt: The original connect is compared against a reconnect that must recover state

blocks.text: The very first connection happens once, deliberately, when a session begins.
A reconnection happens unexpectedly, in response to a failure, and usually needs to re-run the full initialize handshake from scratch, since nothing about the old session state survives the drop.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If you find yourself trying to preserve old session state across a reconnect, you are working against the grain of how MCP sessions are designed.

blocks.text: Treat every reconnect as a fresh start, not a resumed conversation.
2. Detecting That a Reconnect Is Needed
This decision usually comes from connection management, covered in the previous lesson, once a connection is confirmed genuinely broken, not just briefly slow.
Reconnecting too eagerly, on every tiny hiccup, wastes effort and can even make a struggling server worse.
This is exactly the degraded versus closed distinction covered in the previous lesson.
This distinction alone prevents a huge amount of unnecessary reconnect churn.
3. Immediate Retry vs Waiting

blocks.alt: Immediate retry is compared against waiting before retrying

blocks.text: Trying again the instant a drop is detected sometimes works, especially for a very brief network blip.
But retrying immediately and repeatedly against a server that is actually down just adds load to an already struggling system.
A brief pause before the very first retry already helps far more than most people expect.
4. Exponential Backoff

blocks.alt: Each failed attempt doubles the wait before the next one

blocks.text: A common pattern waits a short delay before the first retry, then doubles that delay after each failed attempt, up to some maximum.
This spreads out retry attempts over time, giving a struggling server room to recover instead of being hit repeatedly and instantly.
The maximum delay cap keeps the wait from growing unreasonably long even after many failures.
5. Adding Jitter to Avoid Synchronized Retries

blocks.alt: Many clients retrying at once is spread apart by adding random jitter

blocks.text: If many clients all disconnect from the same server at once, and all retry on the exact same backoff schedule, they can end up hammering the server in synchronized waves.
Adding a small random jitter to each delay spreads those retries out more evenly.
Even a small amount of randomness meaningfully smooths out the retry pattern across many clients.
6. Capping the Number of Attempts

blocks.alt: Attempts under the cap keep retrying while attempts over the cap give up

blocks.text: Retrying forever is rarely the right answer.
A sensible cap, after which the client gives up and surfaces a clear failure, prevents an application from silently hanging indefinitely against a server that is never coming back.

blocks.title: A sensible default
blocks.content: Five attempts with exponential backoff usually covers the vast majority of genuinely temporary outages without waiting excessively long.

blocks.text: 7. Resuming a Session vs Starting Fresh

blocks.alt: Resuming a session is compared against starting a fresh session

blocks.text: Most MCP sessions, per the ephemeral design covered in the Session Lifecycle lesson, simply start over after a reconnect, a fresh initialize handshake, no attempt to resume exactly where things left off.
This keeps reconnection logic simple and predictable.

code.content:
# after reconnecting, discovery has to happen again too
client.initialize()
tools = client.list_tools()   # cannot assume the old list is still valid

blocks.text: 8. What Happens to Requests That Were In Flight
Any request that was still waiting for a response when the connection dropped needs to be treated as failed.
A client should reject those pending requests clearly, rather than leaving them hanging indefinitely while a reconnect happens in the background.
Silently dropping these without telling anyone leaves calling code waiting on a promise that will never resolve.
9. Idempotency Still Matters Here

blocks.alt: A retried request must produce the same result as the original

blocks.text: If a client decides to automatically retry a specific failed request after reconnecting, the same idempotency concerns from the Requests lesson apply directly.
A read is usually safe to retry, a payment is not, without additional safeguards.
Skipping this check is exactly how a naive retry policy can accidentally send the same email twice.
When in doubt, treat the retried request as unsafe and let a human or the model decide instead.
10. Reconnection for Local vs Remote Servers
A local server that crashed usually needs to be relaunched as a new subprocess entirely.
A remote server usually just needs a fresh network connection, the underlying service itself is likely still running the whole time.

blocks.text: This is exactly why the local versus remote lessons earlier in this module matter directly here too.
Neither case is inherently harder, they just call for slightly different recovery code.
11. Surfacing Reconnection Attempts to the User
A brief reconnecting indicator, rather than a confusing frozen interface, keeps a user informed without alarming them over something that often resolves in seconds.

blocks.text: 12. Reconnection for Autonomous Agents
An unattended agent has nobody to notice a frozen interface.
It needs its reconnection logic to be fully automatic, with a sensible cap, so a permanently dead server does not leave the agent stuck forever.
A well designed agent framework treats a maxed out reconnect attempt as a clear, loggable task failure rather than an invisible stall.
13. Logging Reconnection Attempts
Recording every attempt, its delay, and its outcome builds a clear picture of how reliable a given server connection actually is over time.
This same log feeds naturally into the metrics discussed in the Connection Management lesson.
A server that needs frequent reconnects deserves closer investigation, this log is where that pattern first becomes visible.
14. A Worked Example
Trace a client detecting a drop, backing off, and successfully reconnecting on its second attempt.
If every attempt failed, this loop would eventually exit the while condition and the caller would need to handle that final failure.
The doubling delay between attempts is what keeps this from becoming a tight, wasteful retry loop.
15. Common Mistakes in Reconnection Handling

items: Retrying immediately and repeatedly with no backoff at all, adding load to a struggling server.
Retrying forever with no cap, hanging an application indefinitely.
Forgetting to fail pending requests cleanly when a drop is first detected.
Automatically retrying a non-idempotent request without considering the risk of a duplicate action.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is applying the same aggressive retry policy to every kind of failure, rather than distinguishing a brief network blip from a server that is clearly gone for good.
This blanket approach either wastes time waiting on something unrecoverable or gives up too soon on something that would have quickly resolved.
16. Practice: Implement Backoff With a Cap
Write a reconnect loop with exponential backoff, a maximum delay, and a maximum number of attempts before giving up entirely.
Test your implementation against a fake connect function that fails exactly three times before succeeding, and confirm it recovers correctly.
Also confirm it raises a clear final error once every attempt has been exhausted.
Key Takeaway
A good reconnection strategy waits sensibly between attempts, backs off as failures continue, and eventually gives up cleanly rather than retrying forever.

This lesson builds directly on Connection Management from earlier in this module, and connects forward to Timeouts next, which covers how long a client should wait before deciding a single request has failed in the first place.

The autonomous agent point from the newly added section matters especially for background systems, a sensible cap is the only thing standing between a temporary outage and a permanently stuck process.
